title: IIHS study of US police-reported crashes links automatic emergency braking with pedestrian detection to 25% to 27% lower pedestrian crash risk
summary: An IIHS study of US police-reported crashes found that automatic emergency braking with pedestrian detection cut pedestrian crash risk by 25% to 27% and injury crash risk by 29% to 30%.
account: Jessica Cicchino of the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) in Arlington, Virginia, studied police-reported pedestrian crashes in the United States. She compared vehicles with and without automatic emergency braking (AEB) that detects pedestrians, and she used only models on which the system was an optional feature. She estimated crash rates per insured vehicle year and checked them with a second method that compares pedestrian crashes with a crash type that the system cannot affect. Vehicles with the system had a 25% to 27% lower pedestrian crash risk and a 29% to 30% lower pedestrian injury crash risk. Accident Analysis & Prevention published the study online on 14 May 2022. The study found no evidence of a benefit at night on roads without street lighting or at speed limits of 50 mph or more. It also found no evidence of a benefit when the equipped vehicle was turning. The design is observational, and the abstract does not name the makers or describe the detection software.
purpose: Pedestrian detection systems are built to warn drivers of a likely collision with a pedestrian, and many brake automatically when a crash is imminent. The lower crash risk that the study measured was that purpose.
system: Automatic emergency braking (AEB) with pedestrian detection, offered as an optional feature on US passenger vehicle models
developer: Multiple automakers (not named in the abstract)

brief: Jessica Cicchino of the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety measured what automatic emergency braking that detects pedestrians does for people on foot in the United States. Using police-reported crashes, she compared vehicles of the same models with and without the optional system. She found that vehicles with the system had a 25% to 27% lower pedestrian crash risk and a 29% to 30% lower pedestrian injury crash risk.[1] She also reported where she found no evidence of benefit: at night on unlit roads, and at speed limits of 50 mph or more. Nor did she find evidence of benefit when the equipped vehicle was turning. The design is observational, and the abstract names no makers and describes no detection software.[2] Later studies from Japan and from Australia and New Zealand also reported benefits. Automatic emergency braking in some Nissan cars has drawn complaints of false braking that endangered occupants and other road users.
